notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 1 Corinthians 16, drawn from the sources accessed.

---

## 1 Corinthians 16 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *"Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia:"*

- **"Now concerning"** (Greek *peri de*) is a formula Paul uses repeatedly in this letter (cf. 7:1, 8:1, 12:1), indicating he is replying to a question the Corinthians had asked him.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"The collection for the saints"** refers to a relief fund for the impoverished Christians in Jerusalem. Paul mentions this effort in several other passages (Acts 11:27–30; 24:17; Romans 15:26; 2 Corinthians 8–9). The Jerusalem church had particular needs: they supported many widows (Acts 6:1–6), had suffered through famine (Acts 11:27–30), and their early experiment in communal sharing of goods had left many economically vulnerable. The Pulpit Commentary adds that the "enthusiastic communism" of the earliest Jerusalem church had soon ceased, being "an impossible experiment under the conditions which regulate all human life."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **The Greek word for "collection" is *logia***, meaning "an extra collection" — one that is voluntary, not a tax. Paul commanded the churches to take up an offering, but left individual giving to each person's conscience. Precept Austin notes Paul uses at least seven different words for this collection across his letters, including *charis* (grace/gift), *koinonia* (fellowship/sharing), and *diakonia* (service/ministry).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

- Paul had **"directed the churches of Galatia"** — not in his extant letter to the Galatians, but likely during a visit (Acts 18:23) or by a lost letter. Bengel notes Paul's method: "To the Corinthians he proposes the example of the Galatians; to the Macedonians the example of the Corinthians; to the Romans that of the Macedonians and Corinthians. Great is the power of example."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **John MacArthur** (cited at Precept Austin) notes that beyond meeting economic needs, Paul wanted this collection to express the spiritual oneness of the church — Gentiles giving to Jews would strengthen the bond between the two groups (cf. Eph 2:11–18).
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

---

### v. 2: *"On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed."*

- **"On the first day of the week"**: This reflects the early Christian practice of gathering on Sunday (the Lord's Day, Rev 1:10), not the Jewish Sabbath (Saturday). The Christians met on the day of Christ's resurrection (Luke 24:1; John 20:19, 26; Acts 20:7). Gill notes Justin Martyr and Tertullian confirm that in the generation after the apostles, churches collected for the needy after worship on Sunday.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

- The Pulpit Commentary, however, cautions that this verse alone "can hardly be said to imply any religious observance of the Sunday," which rests more on other passages (Acts 20:7; Rev 1:10; John 20:19, 26).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"Each of you should set aside a portion... saving it up"**: The Greek implies setting aside at home, privately, week by week — not in a collection plate at a meeting. Chrysostom suggested this was because some gifts might be so small the donor would be ashamed to make them publicly. Christians should prayerfully determine their gift at home, resisting manipulation. The present imperative "put aside" commands habitual, regular giving.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

- **"As he may prosper"** (Greek *euodoo*, literally "as he has a good journey"): Giving is to be proportionate. No specific percentage (such as a tithe) is stipulated. As one commentator put it, "A tenth is little for some, impossible for others; but week by week each would see how much or how little he had got, and would act accordingly."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

- **"No collections when I come"**: Paul did not want high-pressure, last-minute fundraising in his presence. He wanted giving from the heart, not in response to an apostolic visit. He also had other, higher matters to attend to when he arrived.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

- **Precept Austin summarizes** the principles: giving should be regular (first day), individual (each one), systematic (put aside habitually), and proportionate (as prospered).
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

---

### v. 3: *"Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem."*

- The more accurate rendering is **"whomever you approve, these I will send with letters"** — letters of commendation (cf. Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1; 2 Cor 3:1) introducing the delegates to the Jerusalem church. The KJV's "by your letters" is a mistranslation that obscures the fact that Paul wrote many letters no longer extant.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- Paul wanted **representatives chosen by the Corinthians themselves** to carry the gift. This ensured transparency and kept Paul above reproach in financial matters (cf. 2 Cor 8:20–21). The Corinthian church's autonomy was respected.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-corinthians-16.html

- **"Your gift"** translates *charis* — literally "grace." Paul calls it this "because it flowed from their free love towards their poor brethren… or because their sense of the free love and grace of God to them, was that which moved them to that charitable act" (Poole).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

---

### v. 4: *"And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me."*

- Paul would accompany the delegation **only if the collection was substantial enough** to justify his time and expense. The Pulpit Commentary: "Unless the collection were a substantial proof of the generosity of the Gentile Churches, it would be hardly worth while for St. Paul to go too." Hodge's Commentary agrees: "If the collection be of an amount to make it proper for the apostle also to go with it to Jerusalem."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-16.html

- Under no circumstances would Paul take charge of the money himself. In the end, the collection was adequate and Paul did accompany the delegates (Romans 15:25; Acts 20:4).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 5: *"After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia."*

- Paul had originally intended to sail directly from Ephesus to Corinth, then go to Macedonia, then return to Corinth (2 Cor 1:15–16). **He changed that plan** because the church's disorganization meant a visit would require painful severity, which he hoped to avoid by writing first (2 Cor 1:23–2:1). The Corinthians later accused him of levity over this change; he defends himself in 2 Corinthians.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- Gill notes Paul was at Ephesus, not Philippi when writing (contrary to the spurious subscription added in later manuscripts).
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### vv. 6–7: *"Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits."*

- Paul did eventually **spend three months in Greece** (Acts 20:3–6), fulfilling this intention.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"Help me on my journey"**: It was ancient custom to accompany a departing guest for part of the journey and to supply provisions (Acts 15:3; 17:15; Rom 15:24). The "ye" is emphatic — receiving this favour from the Corinthians would be a sign of affection.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"If the Lord permits"**: Paul habitually submitted all his plans to God's will (cf. James 4:15). G. Campbell Morgan notes: "I know the fascination of having a programme, and having everything in order, and knowing where we are going; but let us leave room, at any rate, for the interference of God."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

---

### vv. 8–9: *"But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me."*

- **Pentecost** is mentioned as a time-marker, not because Paul observed it as a Christian festival. He later desired to be at Jerusalem by Pentecost (Acts 20:16) because the crowds would give him opportunities to preach.
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"A great door for effective work"**: The metaphor of an "open door" for gospel opportunity appears elsewhere (2 Cor 2:12; Col 4:3; Acts 14:27; Rev 3:8). At Ephesus, many were hearing and believing (Acts 19:8–10).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"Many oppose me"**: Acts 19 records both the opportunities and opposition Paul faced at Ephesus — disputing Jews, the silversmith Demetrius stirring up a riot. Paul saw opposition not as a reason to leave but as confirmation that God was at work.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### vv. 10–11: *"If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers."*

- Timothy was young (1 Tim 4:12), of a **timid and sensitive disposition** (1 Tim 5:21–23; 2 Tim 1:6–8). He may well have shrunk from facing the haughty, disputatious Corinthians. Paul's appeal is designed to protect him.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- The Corinthians had already shown they could **despise apostolic authority**; what might they do to a young man like Timothy? Paul grounds his request in the fact that Timothy "does the work of the Lord, just as I am" — the same gospel work, same Lord, same cause.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"Send him on his way in peace"**: This implies not only a peaceful departure but providing for his journey — the same honour shown to those who labour in the word.
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 12: *"Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity."*

- The Corinthians had apparently **requested Apollos** in their letter. Paul "strongly urged" (*parekalesa polla* — "I besought him much") but Apollos declined. This reveals that early church leadership was **not strictly hierarchical**; Paul did not command Apollos.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests Apollos refused **because his name had been abused for party faction** (1 Cor 1:12; 3:5). His refusal to go was noble — he would not fuel the divisions. "Both he and Apollos here show themselves in the purest light."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 13: *"Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong."*

- These **brief, impetuous imperatives** show a sudden burst of emotion as Paul draws the letter to a close (Pulpit). Chrysostom said the Corinthians needed all these exhortations because they were, in Christian matters, "drowsy, unstable, effeminate, and factions."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- Adam Clarke interprets all four as **military metaphors**:
  - **"Watch"** = keep scouts out, sentinels at their posts, lest enemies surprise you.
  - **"Stand fast in the faith"** = keep your ranks, stay close together; if the enemy breaks your ranks, your rout is inevitable.
  - **"Be men of courage"** (*andrizomai*, literally "act like a man") = when attacked, do not flinch; maintain your ground; press forward; strike home.
  - **"Be strong"** = if one division is opposed by too great a force, strengthen that division; summon up all your courage.
  — https://biblehub.com/study/1_corinthians/16-13.htm

- **"Be men of courage"** (*andrizesthe*) occurs **only here in the New Testament**. It appears in the Septuagint at Joshua 1:6–7, 9, 18 — God's charge to Joshua. The KJV's "quit you like men" captures the sense well.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://biblehub.com/study/1_corinthians/16-13.htm

- Gill elaborates: "Watch" means vigilance over self, over fellow believers, against sin, Satan, the world, and false teachers. "Stand fast in the faith" means steadfastness in both the grace of faith and the doctrine of faith.
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 14: *"Do everything in love."*

- All the watching, standing, bravery, and strength **mean nothing without love** (cf. 1 Corinthians 13). The Corinthians are called to do all these things in a meek, humble spirit of love. The Pulpit Commentary connects this to 1 Peter 4:8: "Above all things, have fervent love among yourselves."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### vv. 15–16: *"You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers, to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer."*

- **Stephanas and his household** were among the first converts in Achaia, baptized by Paul himself (1 Cor 1:16). The Pulpit Commentary suggests this paragraph was written lest the Corinthians be angry with Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus for having carried to Paul the bad report about the church's divisions (cf. 1 Cor 1:11 — possibly they were from Chloe's household).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"Submit to such as these"**: Even if they were slaves or freedmen in earthly rank, their Christian devotion and service merited respect and submission from the church.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### vv. 17–18: *"I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men."*

- These three men had come to Paul in Ephesus, likely **bringing the Corinthians' letter of questions** to which Paul now replies. Their visit ministered to Paul in ways the Corinthian church as a whole had failed to do.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"Supplied what was lacking from you"** (literally, "filled up your deficiency"): The Pulpit Commentary notes this is not a rebuke but a tender expression — "the void caused by your absence." They represented the Corinthians and refreshed Paul's spirit by telling him about them.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **Fortunatus** is possibly the same man later mentioned in Clement's epistle to the Corinthians (c. AD 96) as the bearer of that letter. The names Fortunatus and Achaicus were common among slaves or freedmen.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

---

### v. 19: *"The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house."*

- **"The churches of Asia"** = congregations in Proconsular Asia (western Asia Minor), centered on Ephesus. Constant trade and travel between Ephesus and Corinth made these greetings natural.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **Aquila and Priscilla** (Prisca): This married couple had ministered with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:1–3), then travelled with him to Ephesus (Acts 18:24–28). They were Paul's partners in tent-making and hosted a church in their home.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"The church that meets at their house"**: House churches were the norm until the third century. Morris notes a moderately well-to-do home's entertaining room could hold about 30 people. In any city there were likely multiple house churches.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

---

### v. 20: *"All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss."*

- **"A holy kiss"**: This was the kiss of peace (cf. Rom 16:16; 2 Cor 13:12; 1 Pet 5:14), a sign of reconciliation and Christian love, rooted in Jewish and early Christian custom. John Trapp quips it was "not hollow, as Joab and Judas; not carnal, as that harlot, Proverbs 7:13."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that **the practice was later abolished** due to abuse and "hideous heathen calumnies" (rumours of immorality at Christian gatherings). In the Roman Catholic Church, a vestige remains in the custom of kissing the *pax* (a tablet or crucifix) passed among the congregation. In the Eastern Orthodox Church, the kiss of peace is still exchanged at Easter with the greeting "Christ is risen!"
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 21: *"This greeting is in my own hand—Paul."*

- Paul customarily **dictated his letters to a secretary** (amanuensis), then added a personal greeting in his own handwriting (cf. Gal 6:11; Col 4:18; 2 Thess 3:17). The Pulpit Commentary suggests Paul's "thorn in the flesh" may have been acute ophthalmia (eye disease), which inclined him to use a secretary. When he did write, his letters were large and straggling (Gal 6:11).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- The autograph also served as an **authentication mark** against forged letters, which became a problem (2 Thess 2:2; 3:17).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### v. 22: *"If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!"*

- This verse is particularly solemn because it comes **in Paul's own handwriting**. The Greek *anathema* translates the Hebrew *cherem* — something devoted to destruction (Lev 27:29; Josh 6:17). In Jewish practice, *anathema* was the **third and final level of synagogue discipline**, after which all hope of reconciliation was cut off. The person could never be reconciled to the synagogue and was no longer accounted a Jew at all.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- The Pulpit Commentary expresses **discomfort with a harsh reading**: "I cannot pretend to understand what St. Paul means by it, unless it be 'Let personal love to Christ be the essential of Christian fellowship, and let him who has it not be regarded as apart from the Church.'" The writer argues a severe imprecation would be "the very antithesis to the general tone of the apostle" and notes that Jewish *cherem* could refer to milder, temporary forms of excommunication. Even "handing over to Satan" (1 Cor 5:5; 1 Tim 1:20) was merciful in purpose.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"The Lord"** in "does not love the Lord" is literally "the Lord Jesus Christ" — the full title, emphasising His identity. Poole notes that "love is an affection of the heart, but discernible by overt acts."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- **"Come, O Lord!"** translates the Aramaic ***Marana tha*** (or *Maran atha* — "Our Lord, come!" or "Our Lord has come"). This was one of the earliest words of the Christian vocabulary, an eschatological prayer preserved in its original Aramaic even in Greek-speaking churches. The Pulpit Commentary notes it is "like the Jewish *shem atha*, 'the Name cometh'" and may allude to Malachi 4:6, with which the Old Testament ends.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

### vv. 23–24: *"The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen."*

- **"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you"** is a *gnorisma* or "badge of confidence" found in some form at the end of every Pauline epistle. Paul pronounces a blessing of grace over people he had to rebuke strongly — showing his apostolic authority flowed from love, not severity.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

- **"My love be with you all in Christ Jesus"**: Gill notes this is spiritual affection — "in Christ, and for his sake" — not merely natural fondness. Paul's final word before the Amen is "Jesus," emphasising Him from beginning to end.
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/

- The **Amen** is possibly genuine, though omitted by some early manuscripts (B, F, G). The spurious subscription found in later manuscripts (claiming the letter was "written from Philippi" and sent "by Timothy") is "absolutely erroneous" — the letter was written from Ephesus (v. 8), and Timothy was not the bearer.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

---

## Denominational and Other Distinctives

### On Giving and the Tithe (vv. 1–2)

The consensus across the Protestant commentaries consulted (Enduring Word/Pentecostal-charismatic, Precept Austin/evangelical, Gill/Baptist, Pulpit/Anglican) is that this passage teaches **voluntary, proportionate, systematic giving** — not a mandatory tithe. MacArthur (cited at Precept Austin) states: "No amount or percentage is ever required in the New Testament. Rather, each believer is to give from his heart." The "as he may prosper" principle is understood across traditions to mean giving in proportion to one's income, not a fixed tenth.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-16-commentary

### On Sunday Worship (v. 2)

Most Protestant traditions see in this verse evidence that the early church met for worship on Sunday, the first day of the week, rather than the Jewish Sabbath. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) offers a more cautious reading — that this verse alone "can hardly be said to imply any religious observance of the Sunday," which rests more firmly on Acts 20:7, Revelation 1:10, and the resurrection appearances. Seventh-day Sabbatarian traditions would differ strongly, though no Sabbatarian source was in the permitted list.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

### On the Holy Kiss (v. 20)

The **Pulpit Commentary** (Anglican) notes that the practice was discontinued in most churches due to abuses and pagan slander. It records that the **Roman Catholic Church** retains a vestige in kissing the *pax* (a tablet or crucifix kissed by the priest then passed among the congregation), while the **Eastern Orthodox Church** retains the actual kiss of peace at Easter ("Christ is risen!"). Most Protestant traditions interpret this as a culturally-bound expression of Christian love, fulfilled today by handshakes or other warm greetings.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

### On "Anathema Maranatha" (v. 22)

The **Pulpit Commentary** (Anglican) offers the most distinctive reading, expressing difficulty with traditional interpretations of this verse as a harsh imprecation. The writer suggests it means that "personal love to Christ be the essential of Christian fellowship" and that the one without it be "regarded as apart from the Church" — aligning it more with excommunication for redemptive purposes (like 1 Cor 5:5) than with a final curse.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_corinthians/16.htm

**Gill** (Baptist) reads it more straightforwardly as a solemn warning: those who do not love Christ, living and dying so, "he wishes they may be accursed at the coming of the Lord."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/16.htm

**Enduring Word** (Pentecostal-charismatic) interprets *anathema* against its Jewish background as the third and final level of synagogue discipline — a grave pronouncement on those who claim Jesus but have no genuine love for Him.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-16/
